c.tagline: Andean colonial jewel of blue domes, cobblestones, and Panama hats.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered by law; make sure the driver uses the taxímetro, as short rides across the center run only a few dollars. Uber and InDrive both operate but coverage is limited.

emergency.note: 911 is the unified national emergency number (ECU 911) connecting to police, fire, and ambulance across Ecuador.

solo.f: Safety index is the main factor (65/100)

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing occurs around Mercado 9 de Octubre, Feria Libre market and the Terminal Terrestre, especially after dark.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed colonial core of cobblestone streets, red-tiled roofs, and the blue-domed New Cathedral (Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción) rising over Parque Calderón; best for first-timers who want every church, market, and museum within walking distance.

A modern, leafy residential district just south of the Tomebamba River with tree-lined avenues, cafes, and easy access to both the old town and the university; a convenient, central base for longer stays.
A historic western old-town neighborhood around Plaza de San Sebastián and the Museo de Arte Moderno, with an artsy, gallery-and-plaza feel and quieter streets than the center.

water.note: Cuenca's municipal tap water is treated and among the few in South America considered safe to drink.

transit.hours: The Tranvía runs roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; city buses run from around 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM, with taxis and ride apps filling late-night gaps.
transit.note: Cuenca's modern Tranvía light-rail line (opened 2020) runs a single route across the city, including a stop at the airport, complemented by an extensive municipal bus network.
transit.pay: Buses and the Tranvía use a rechargeable card or contactless fare (around $0.35 per ride); exact cash is also accepted on buses. As Ecuador uses the US dollar, small bills and coins are handy.

bus: Intercity coaches from Terminal Terrestre to Guayaquil, Quito, and Loja
train: No passenger rail service (Ecuador's tourist trains are currently suspended)

tip.r: Not obligatory; a 10% service charge is often already added at sit-down restaurants, and rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Hornado
food.desc: Whole pig slow-roasted overnight, hand-pulled to order and piled with mote, llapingacho potato cakes and pickled onion encurtido.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: Upstairs food hall where rows of cooks carve hornado all morning; busiest at weekends.

places.name: Mercado 9 de Octubre
places.note: Smaller central market with early-morning hornado and juice counters.

places.name: Feria Libre El Arenal
places.note: Cuenca's biggest market; cheapest plates and the most local crowd.

food.name: Mote pillo
food.desc: The definitive Cuencano plate: hominy corn sauteed with egg, onion, milk and cilantro, eaten at breakfast or beside roast pork.

places.name: Raymipampa
places.note: Institution on the main square since the 1980s, serving Cuencan classics all day.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: A couple of dollars a plate at the market counters, cooked to order.

places.name: El Maiz
places.note: Traditional Ecuadorian kitchen focused on corn dishes, in a colonial house near the river.

food.name: Cuy asado
food.desc: Guinea pig spit-roasted over charcoal until the skin crackles, an Andean celebration dish served with potatoes and aji.

places.name: Guajibamba
places.note: The city's best-known cuy restaurant; order ahead as it is roasted whole.

places.name: Tres Estrellas
places.note: Long-running family restaurant doing cuy and other Cuencan specialities.

places.name: Feria Libre El Arenal
places.note: Weekend stalls turning cuy on charcoal at market prices.

food.name: Humitas and tamales
food.desc: Fresh ground corn beaten with eggs, cheese and butter, wrapped in the husk and steamed; the Andean answer to afternoon coffee.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: Steamed humitas and quimbolitos sold warm from covered baskets.

places.name: Raymipampa
places.note: Reliable sit-down option for humitas with hot coffee or chocolate.

places.name: Mercado 9 de Octubre
places.note: Morning stalls with humitas, tamales and fresh cheese.

food.name: Cascaritas
food.desc: A Cuenca street ritual: pork skin blowtorched golden on the carcass, chopped straight onto paper and eaten with lime and salt.

places.name: Feria Libre El Arenal
places.note: Weekend cascarita vendors working the pork carcasses in the open air.

places.name: Mercado 9 de Octubre
places.note: Central, easier-to-find version of the same weekend pork ritual.

food.name: Dulces de Corpus
food.desc: Convent-rooted sweets - alfajores, quesitos, huevos de faltriquera, cocadas - piled on stands for the week-long Corpus Christi fair in June.

places.name: Corpus Christi fair, Parque Calderon
places.note: Every June the cathedral square fills with tiered stands of traditional sweets.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: Sweet vendors sell many of the same dulces year-round.

places.name: Bakeries along Calle Bolivar
places.note: Colonial-street panaderias with cocadas, alfajores and quesadillas.

food.name: Canelazo
food.desc: Hot Andean nightcap of cinnamon and naranjilla infusion spiked with sugarcane aguardiente, essential in Cuenca's cool 2,500m evenings.

places.name: Wunderbar Cafe
places.note: Long-established terrace bar on the stairway down to the Tomebamba river.

places.name: Tres Estrellas
places.note: Traditional restaurant pouring canelazo with the Cuencan menu.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: Market counters serve hot canelazo and morocho on chilly mornings.

food.name: Horchata cuencana
food.desc: Deep pink herbal infusion of up to 30 Andean flowers and herbs, served hot with lime; nothing like Mexican rice horchata.

places.name: Mercado 10 de Agosto
places.note: Herb vendors brew it fresh and sell the dried flower bundles to take home.

places.name: Feria Libre El Arenal
places.note: Rows of herbalists mixing custom horchata blends by the cup.

places.name: Raymipampa
places.note: Easy central spot for a hot horchata with breakfast.

landmarks: Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción (New Cathedral)
Cuenca's sky-blue domes crown this monumental brick cathedral begun in 1885, whose marble-clad interior and rooftop terrace define the UNESCO-listed historic centre.
Parque Calderón
The palm-shaded main square at the colonial city's heart, framed by both cathedrals, flower sellers and arcaded buildings perfect for people-watching.
Iglesia del Sagrario (Old Cathedral)
Founded in 1557 with Inca stones from Pumapungo, the whitewashed old cathedral is now a museum of religious art and colonial history.
Pumapungo Archaeological Park and Museum
Terraced ruins of the great Inca city of Tomebamba spread beside a free museum of Cañari culture, shrunken heads and Ecuadorian ethnography.
Mirador de Turi
A hilltop church viewpoint south of town where the whole red-tiled sweep of Cuenca and its ring of Andean peaks unfolds, magical at dusk.
El Barranco and Río Tomebamba
Colonial houses teeter dramatically over the grassy banks of the Tomebamba river, linked by stone stairways along Cuenca's most photogenic promenade.
Cajas National Park
Barely an hour west, this high-altitude wilderness of 270 glacial lakes, polylepis forests and moody páramo offers superb day hikes from the city.
Museo del Sombrero de Paja Toquilla (Panama Hat Museum)
Working workshops reveal how Cuenca's famed toquilla-straw Panama hats are woven, blocked and finished, with vintage presses and hats for sale.
Plaza de las Flores
Beside El Carmen church, Ecuador's prettiest flower market fills a tiny colonial square with roses, lilies and herb bundles sold by cholas cuencanas.
Ingapirca
Ecuador's most important Inca site, a day trip north, centres on an elliptical sun temple of exquisite mortarless stonework atop windswept highlands.

train.note: Ecuador's national railway stopped carrying passengers in March 2020 and Ferrocarriles del Ecuador was put into liquidation two months later, with the assets returned to the state; since then only short tourist sections in Imbabura and Chimborazo provinces have reopened. Cuenca's old line towards Sibambe has long been out of use, so no train reaches the city and there is no international rail anywhere in Ecuador. Within the city the Tranvía de Cuenca light-rail line runs through the centre, but it is urban transit rather than an intercity service, so all long-distance travel is by bus or air.

bus.note: Everything leaves from the Terminal Terrestre on Avenida España, about 10 minutes northeast of the old town, where a 10-cent departure fee is collected at the turnstiles. Buses run every hour or two to Guayaquil (3.5-4 hours), Quito (8-10 hours), Loja (4.5-7 hours with Viajeros or San Luis) and Alausí (about 4 hours with Transportes Alausí); tickets are bought at the company windows. Departures for Peru leave in the evening around 19:30, 21:00 and 23:00 and usually involve a change at Machala or Huaquillas, where the joint CEBAF post handles both countries' formalities before you continue to Tumbes and Piura - buy a day ahead in high season.

ferry.note: Cuenca lies at 2,560 m in the southern Andes, straddling four shallow rivers that carry no traffic, and the Pacific is a four-hour drive away; there are no passenger boat services.

half.name: Gualaceo

half.name: Chordeleg
half.blurb: Small artisan town famous for handmade filigree silver jewelry sold in shops ringing its central plaza.

half.name: San Bartolomé
